newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia 1996 trade gap shrinks to 617.97 mln rgt.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia 1996 trade gap shrinks to 617.97 mln rgt.

text.p: Malaysia's 1996 trade deficit shrank to 617.97 million ringgit ($250.19 million) from a gap of 9.36 billion ringgit in 1995, the Statistics Department reported on Tuesday.
In December 1996 alone, Malaysia had a trade surplus of 872 million ringgit, compared with a surplus of 637.34 million in December 1995 and a gap of 526.4 million in November 1996.
The 1996 gap was significantly less than the deficit of 5.2 billion ringgit forecast in the Finance Ministry's Economic Report released last October.
The department said exports last year totalled 196.69 billion ringgit, up by 6.3 percent from 1995. Imports were 197.31 billion ringgit, up by 1.5 percent from 1995.
Exports for December 1996 totalled 17.103 billion ringgit compared with 16.5 billion ringgit in November 1996 and 17.504 billion ringgit in December 1995.
Imports in December 1996 totalled 16.231 billion ringgit against 17.0 billion ringgit in November 1996 and 16.867 billion ringgit in December 1996, the department said.
The department said exports of manufactured goods continued to grow strongly while the major primary commodities showed a mixed performance.
It said electronic parts continued to be the leading export earners in 1996 with receipts totalling 35.2 billion ringgit or 17.9 percent of total export earnings.

The second biggest revenue earner was palm oil with exports of 9.4 billion ringgit or 4.8 percent of total exports. But compared with 1995, palm oil exports dropped 10.2 percent or 1.1 billion ringgit.
The major export markets were Singapore (40.3 billion ringgit), the United States (35.8 billion ringgit), Japan (26.4 billion ringgit) and Hong Kong (11.6 billion ringgit).
Singapore, the United States and Japan alone accounted for 52.1 percent of the country's total exports.
The department said the biggest contributor to the increased level of imports in 1996 was machinery and transport equipment, which rose 1.4 percent or 1.6 billion ringgit.
Machinery and transport equipment was also the largest import component, accounting for 60 percent or 118.4 billion ringgit, the department said.
It said "lumpy" imports comprising vessels, floating structures, aircraft and associated equipment totalled 5.8 billion ringgit.

Economists welcomed the improvement in the 1996 trade figures, but warned that such gains may be less dramatic this year as Malaysia rushes to finish large infrastructure projects in time for the 1998 Commonwealth Games, which it is hosting.

"My view is that the improvement in 1997 will be harder to come by," said Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at J.M. Sassoon & Co. "I think they (the Malaysian government) have tried to hold some of the imports last year because of the current account (deficit)." ($1=2.47 ringgit)
